note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/05 Chemical energetics/5.1 Enthalpy change, ΔH.md
outline: Reactions transfer energy through bond breaking and making. Exothermic changes have $\Delta H<0$; endothermic changes have $\Delta H>0$. On a pathway diagram, activation energy reaches the peak from reactants, while $\Delta H$ compares products with reactants. Standard conditions here are $298\,\mathrm K$ and $101\,\mathrm{kPa}$. Formation, combustion and neutralisation enthalpies refer to one mole of product, fuel and water respectively. Bond-energy estimates use energy of bonds broken minus energy of bonds formed; averages need not equal exact values. Calorimetry uses $q=mc\Delta T$ for the solution, then $\Delta H=-q/n$ for the reaction.

misconceptions.statement: A reaction that makes its surroundings warm has positive $\Delta H$.
misconceptions.refutation: Heat leaves an exothermic reacting system, so the products have lower enthalpy and $\Delta H<0$.
misconceptions.contrast: A heat pad warms the surroundings: its reaction is exothermic and has negative $\Delta H$.

misconceptions.statement: Activation energy and enthalpy change are the same vertical gap on a pathway diagram.
misconceptions.refutation: Activation energy goes from reactants to the peak; $\Delta H$ goes from reactants to products.

misconceptions.statement: Standard conditions alone define standard enthalpy of formation.
misconceptions.refutation: The elements must also be in their standard states, and exactly one mole of product must form.
misconceptions.contrast: Carbon in its standard state is graphite, not gaseous carbon atoms.

misconceptions.statement: Neutralisation enthalpy is quoted per mole of acid or per reaction as written.
misconceptions.refutation: It is the enthalpy change when an acid and an alkali react to form one mole of water.
misconceptions.contrast: If an equation forms two moles of water, divide its enthalpy change by two.

misconceptions.statement: Breaking bonds releases energy while making bonds takes in energy.
misconceptions.refutation: Bond breaking requires energy; bond making releases energy.
misconceptions.contrast: A reaction is exothermic when forming bonds releases more than breaking bonds absorbs.

misconceptions.statement: Bond energy calculations add the energies of bonds formed to those broken.
misconceptions.refutation: Use $\Delta H=\sum E(\text{broken})-\sum E(\text{formed})$ and count bonds using the balanced equation.
misconceptions.contrast: For $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$, break one H–H and one Cl–Cl, then form two H–Cl bonds.

misconceptions.statement: Every C–H bond in every molecule has the same exact bond energy.
misconceptions.refutation: Bond energy varies with molecular environment. A tabulated average bond energy averages values across compounds; a specified bond dissociation enthalpy is exact for that gaseous process.
misconceptions.contrast: The mean of the four successive C–H dissociations in methane is not the first dissociation alone.

misconceptions.statement: Use fuel mass in $q=mc\Delta T$, or use Celsius temperature as an absolute temperature.
misconceptions.refutation: Use the mass of the heated water or solution and the temperature difference. For a heat-releasing reaction, divide negative heat absorbed by moles reacted.
misconceptions.contrast: A change of $10\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ is $10\,\mathrm K$, not $283\,\mathrm K$.

worked.problem: A pathway has reactants at 20, products at 50 and peak at 100 kJ mol$^{-1}$. Find forward activation energy.

steps.do: Read the reactant and peak levels: 20 and 100 kJ mol$^{-1}$.
steps.why: Activation energy is measured from the starting level to the peak.
Subtract the reactant level; a barrier cannot be negative.

worked.problem: Estimate $\Delta H$ for $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$ using 436, 242 and 431 kJ mol$^{-1}$ for H–H, Cl–Cl and H–Cl.

steps.do: Broken: one H–H and one Cl–Cl, so $436+242=678$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
steps.why: The balanced equation fixes the bond counts.

steps.do: Formed: two H–Cl, so $2(431)=862$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
steps.why: Each product molecule contains one H–Cl bond.
Energy absorbed for breaking minus energy released in forming sets the sign.

worked.problem: A reaction warms 100 g of water by 5.0 K; 0.020 mol reacts. Calculate $\Delta H$, with $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.

steps.why: Use the mass of water and the temperature difference.
The reaction releases the heat absorbed by water; divide by moles and convert to kJ.

items.stem:
A student mixes 25.0 cm³ of 0.350 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution with 25.0 cm³ of
0.350 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. The temperature increases by 2.5 °C. No heat is lost to the
surroundings.
The final mixture has a specific heat capacity of 4.2 J cm⁻³
K⁻¹.

items.explanation: The mixture absorbs $50.0\times4.2\times2.5=525$ J. $n=0.0250\times0.350=0.00875$ mol, hence $\Delta H=-0.525/0.00875=-60$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; C effectively uses the wrong mole count.

$E_a$(reverse) = peak enthalpy − product enthalpy.

items.stem: For $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$, use H–H = [[hh]], Cl–Cl = [[cc]] and H–Cl = [[hc]] kJ mol$^{-1}$. Calculate $\Delta H$ in kJ mol$^{-1}$.
items.explanation: Break one H–H and one Cl–Cl bond; form two H–Cl bonds. Subtract the latter total from the former.
hints: Bond breaking takes in energy and bond making gives it out.
From the equation: one H–H and one Cl–Cl bond break, and two H–Cl bonds form.
$\Delta H$ = (energy of bonds broken) − (energy of bonds formed) = (H–H + Cl–Cl) − 2 × (H–Cl).

items.stem: For $\ce{CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl}$, C–H = [[ch]], Cl–Cl = [[cc]], C–Cl = [[ccl]] and H–Cl = [[hcl]] kJ mol$^{-1}$. Calculate the bond-energy estimate of $\Delta H$.
items.explanation: Only one C–H and one Cl–Cl bond break; one C–Cl and one H–Cl bond form. Average bond energies give an estimate.
hints: Count only the bonds that change; three of the four C–H bonds in methane are untouched.
One C–H and one Cl–Cl bond break; one C–Cl and one H–Cl bond form.

9701-5.1.1.establish: Enthalpy change is the heat transferred at constant pressure: $\Delta H=H_{\mathrm{products}}-H_{\mathrm{reactants}}$. Exothermic reactions transfer energy from the reacting system to the surroundings; products have lower enthalpy and $\Delta H<0$. Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings; products have higher enthalpy and $\Delta H>0$. The sign describes the reacting system, not the surroundings.
9701-5.1.1.connect: These energy differences become the vertical separations in reaction pathway diagrams.
9701-5.1.1.note:
- Exothermic: energy released to surroundings; $\Delta H<0$.
- Endothermic: energy absorbed from surroundings; $\Delta H>0$.

diagram_descriptions: Exothermic pathway. Vertical axis: energy; horizontal axis: progress of reaction, not time. Reactants form a higher plateau on the left, the curve rises to a peak, then falls to a lower product plateau on the right. The double-headed activation-energy arrow spans reactants to peak. The double-headed enthalpy-change arrow spans reactants to products; its length is a magnitude, while products minus reactants is negative. Reverse activation energy spans products to the same peak.

Endothermic pathway. Vertical axis: energy; horizontal axis: progress of reaction, not time. Reactants are at a low left plateau, the curve rises to a peak, then falls to products at a higher right plateau. The forward activation-energy arrow spans reactants to peak. The enthalpy-change arrow spans the two plateaux and is labelled as positive. Reverse activation energy is the smaller gap from products to peak. Both arrows are double-headed; the level difference fixes the sign.

9701-5.1.3.motivate: An enthalpy value is only useful if you know the conditions and the amount of reaction it describes.
9701-5.1.3.establish: Standard conditions in this syllabus are $298\ \mathrm K$ and $101\ \mathrm{kPa}$, indicated by $\ominus$. A standard state is the most stable physical form under those conditions. Enthalpy change of reaction, $\Delta H_r$, refers to the stoichiometric amounts in the equation. Formation, $\Delta H_f$, forms one mole of compound from its elements. Combustion, $\Delta H_c$, completely burns one mole of substance in oxygen. Neutralisation, $\Delta H_{neut}$, is the enthalpy change when an aqueous acid and aqueous alkali react to form one mole of water. Standard enthalpy changes require standard conditions and standard states; standard formation specifically starts from elements in their standard states. An element in its standard state has standard formation enthalpy zero.
9701-5.1.3.connect: The definition decides which mole amount belongs in the denominator of a calorimetry calculation.
9701-5.1.3.note:
- Standard conditions: $298\ \mathrm K$, $101\ \mathrm{kPa}$; specify standard states.
- Formation: one mole of compound from elements; combustion: one mole completely burned.
- Neutralisation: one mole of water formed; reaction: equation as written.

forms.name: Define an enthalpy change term
wordings: Define standard enthalpy change of combustion.
State what is meant by the standard enthalpy change of formation.
Define the term enthalpy change of neutralisation.
forms.example:
**Define** standard enthalpy change of combustion, $\Delta H_c^\ominus$:

- the enthalpy change when **one mole** of a substance
- is **completely burned in oxygen**
- under **standard conditions** ($298\ \mathrm K$, $101\ \mathrm{kPa}$), with the substances in their standard states.
forms.check: Define the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation.
forms.answer: The enthalpy change when an aqueous acid and an aqueous alkali react to form one mole of water, under standard conditions ($298\ \mathrm K$ and $101\ \mathrm{kPa}$) with substances in their standard states.

forms.name: Link an equation to its enthalpy term and mole basis
wordings: Deduce the standard enthalpy change of formation from the equation and its $\Delta H$.
Identify the enthalpy change shown by the equation.
Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation.
forms.example:
**Given:** $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$, $\Delta H_r^\ominus=-572\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for the equation as written.

- The equation forms two moles of water, so it is a reaction enthalpy and not a formation enthalpy.
- Formation needs **one mole** of compound, so divide by $2$.
- $\Delta H_f^\ominus[\ce{H2O(l)}]=-572\div2=-286\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.
forms.check: $\ce{H2SO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) -> Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l)}$ has $\Delta H=-114\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for the equation as written. Deduce the enthalpy change of neutralisation and explain your working.
forms.answer: Neutralisation is per mole of water formed. The equation forms two moles of water, so $\Delta H_{neut}=-114\div2=-57\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.
forms.source: CAIE 9701 syllabus 5.1.3; Library: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c5.1.pdf p.10-12; CAIE 9701 s22 P11 Q10 examiner report

rubric.point: Neutralisation enthalpy is per mole of water formed.
Divides by two because two moles of water form.

Requires −57 or 57 explicitly described as negative, released or exothermic; unsigned 57 alone does not earn this point. Accept equivalent formatting with sign or qualification attached to this result.

retry.answer: Formation is for one mole of compound. The equation forms two moles of $\ce{Al2O3}$, so $\Delta H_f^\ominus=-3340\div2=-1670\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

forms.name: Classify state-labelled equations and their mole basis
wordings: Identify all applicable named enthalpy changes for each equation.
Explain why the equation must be rescaled before quoting a formation or neutralisation enthalpy.
forms.example: Assume standard conditions. For $\ce{C(s, graphite) + O2(g) -> CO2(g)}$: first check elements in standard states and one mole of compound, so this is formation of carbon dioxide. Next check one mole of carbon completely burned in oxygen, so it is also combustion of carbon. It is also a reaction enthalpy: the classifications overlap. For $\ce{HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)}$, one mole of water forms from aqueous acid and alkali, so the reaction enthalpy is also the neutralisation enthalpy.
forms.check: Assume $298\ \mathrm K$ and $101\ \mathrm{kPa}$ and the states shown. Identify all applicable formation, combustion or neutralisation enthalpies: (i) $\ce{H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> H2O(l)}$; (ii) $\ce{2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s)}$; (iii) $\ce{H2SO4(aq) + 2KOH(aq) -> K2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l)}$. Explain each mole basis and how to rescale where needed.
forms.answer: All three have reaction enthalpies. (i) Formation of liquid water and combustion of hydrogen both apply: one mole of water forms from standard-state elements and one mole of hydrogen burns completely. (ii) The equation as written consumes two moles of magnesium and forms two moles of magnesium oxide: divide its enthalpy by two to obtain either formation of magnesium oxide or combustion of magnesium per mole. (iii) It is an acid–alkali neutralisation reaction; divide its reaction enthalpy by two for neutralisation enthalpy per mole of water. It is neither formation from elements nor combustion.
forms.source: Library: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c5.1.pdf pp.10–12; bundle 9701 w24 P12 Q9, s22 P11 Q10 and s22 P22 Q1 examiner comments

rubric.point: (i) Both formation of liquid water and combustion of hydrogen; one mole of each relevant substance, with elements in standard states.
(ii) Both named molar values require halving; the unscaled equation has two moles of magnesium and oxide.
(iii) Neutralisation is per mole of water, requiring half the reaction enthalpy; not formation or combustion.

retry.check: Under standard conditions classify $\ce{1/2N2(g) + 3/2H2(g) -> NH3(g)}$ and $\ce{2CO(g) + O2(g) -> 2CO2(g)}$. Identify named molar values and any rescaling.
retry.answer: The first is formation of one mole of ammonia from elements in their standard states, and a reaction enthalpy. It is not combustion or neutralisation. The second is a reaction enthalpy; divide by two for combustion enthalpy of carbon monoxide. It is not formation from elements because carbon monoxide is a compound.

rubric.point: Ammonia equation: formation from standard-state elements, one mole formed.

The CO equation has a reaction enthalpy and must be divided by two to give combustion enthalpy per mole of CO; credit this classification and scaling without requiring the word compound. Formation from elements is incorrect.

misconceptions.idea: Standard conditions alone define standard enthalpy of formation.
misconceptions.temptation: The conditions 298 K and 101 kPa seem to be the whole definition.
misconceptions.fix: The elements must also be in their standard states and exactly one mole of compound must form.

misconceptions.idea: Neutralisation enthalpy is quoted per mole of acid or per reaction as written.

misconceptions.fix: The basis is one mole of water formed. If the equation forms two moles of water, divide by two.

9701-5.1.4.motivate: If breaking bonds requires energy, how can a chemical reaction heat its surroundings?
9701-5.1.4.establish: Breaking bonds absorbs energy because bonded atoms must be separated against their attraction. Making bonds releases energy as atoms enter a lower-energy bonded arrangement. Both processes contribute to a reaction. The reaction is exothermic when making product bonds releases more energy than breaking reactant bonds absorbs; it is endothermic when bond breaking requires more than bond making releases.
9701-5.1.4.connect: This energy balance gives the subtraction used in bond-energy calculations.
9701-5.1.4.note:
- Bond breaking absorbs energy; bond making releases energy.
- Compare the total energy absorbed and released to determine the reaction sign.

discover.stem: Which explanation describes an exothermic reaction?

options.A: Breaking bonds releases more than making bonds absorbs.
options.C: Breaking and forming bonds both release energy.
options.D: Making bonds releases more than breaking bonds absorbs.

discover.explanation: Bond breaking always requires energy. Net release occurs because bond formation releases the larger total, not because bond breaking releases heat.

9701-5.1.4.plain_words: Breaking bonds takes in energy and making bonds gives out energy. Every reaction does both. If more energy is released making new bonds than is absorbed breaking old ones, the reaction is exothermic.

forms.name: Explain the sign of enthalpy change using bond breaking and making
wordings: Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why the reaction is exothermic.
Explain why this reaction is endothermic.
Suggest why energy is released overall.
forms.example:
**Explain** why the combustion of methane is exothermic:

- Energy is **absorbed** to break the bonds in methane and oxygen.
- Energy is **released** when the new bonds in carbon dioxide and water form.
- More energy is released making the new bonds than is absorbed breaking the old ones, so the overall change is exothermic.
forms.check: The reaction $\ce{N2(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO(g)}$ has $\Delta H=+180\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Explain, in terms of bonds, why it is endothermic.
forms.answer: Energy is absorbed to break the bonds in nitrogen and oxygen, and energy is released when the bonds in nitrogen monoxide form. More energy is absorbed breaking the bonds than is released making them, so the reaction is endothermic.
forms.source: CAIE 9701 syllabus 5.1.4; Library: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c5.1.pdf p.13; CAIE 9701 w25 P11 Q7

rubric.point: Bond breaking absorbs (needs) energy; bond making releases energy.
Forming bonds in nitrogen monoxide releases energy.

More energy is absorbed in breaking bonds than released in forming bonds; equivalently less energy is released forming bonds than absorbed breaking bonds. Judge the direction: less refers to energy released forming bonds, and more to energy absorbed breaking bonds.

retry.check: A student says: "Hydrogen burns and gives out heat because breaking the bonds in hydrogen and oxygen releases energy." Explain what is wrong and give the correct explanation of why $\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$ is exothermic.
retry.answer: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy; it never releases it. The reaction is exothermic because more energy is released when the O-H bonds in water form than is absorbed when the H-H and O=O bonds break.

rubric.point: States that bond breaking absorbs energy (does not release it).

misconceptions.fix: Bond breaking absorbs energy; bond making releases it. Heat out is the net result of the larger release on bond formation.

9701-5.1.5.motivate: A balanced equation tells you how many bonds contribute, not just which bond types occur.
9701-5.1.5.establish: Use the balanced equation to count every bond broken and formed. Bond energies are positive energies for breaking gaseous bonds. Multiply each bond energy by its bond count, add the broken-bond energies, then subtract the formed-bond total: $\Delta H_r\approx\sum E(\mathrm{broken})-\sum E(\mathrm{formed})$. For $\ce{H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g)}$, break one H–H and one Cl–Cl bond and form two H–Cl bonds. With energies $436$, $242$ and $431\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively, the estimate is $436+242-2(431)=-184\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for the equation as written.
9701-5.1.5.connect: Bond breaking and making explain the subtraction; average data explain why the result is an estimate.
9701-5.1.5.note:
- Count bonds using the balanced equation.
- $\Delta H_r\approx\sum E(\mathrm{broken})-\sum E(\mathrm{formed})$.

forms.name: Calculate enthalpy change of reaction from bond energies
wordings: Use the bond energies in the table to calculate the enthalpy change of the reaction.
Calculate $\Delta H_r$ for the reaction.
Calculate the enthalpy change of the reaction using the data.
forms.example: Calculate $\Delta H_r$ for $\ce{2C2H4(g) + 2H2(g) -> 2C2H6(g)}$ using C=C $612$, H–H $436$, C–C $347$ and C–H $413\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Step 1: draw ethene and ethane; eight C–H bonds occur on both sides and cancel when using the same average value. Step 2: count changed bonds with coefficients: break two C=C and two H–H, costing $2(612)+2(436)=2096$. Form two C–C and four extra C–H, releasing $2(347)+4(413)=2346$. Step 3: broken minus formed gives $2096-2346=-250\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for the equation as written, or $-125\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ per mole of ethene. Counting every bond on both sides gives the same result. C=C uses its supplied double-bond value once per double bond, not twice the C–C single-bond value.
forms.check: Calculate $\Delta H_r$ for $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(g)}$ using $E$(H-H) $=436$, $E$(O=O) $=496$ and $E$(O-H) $=463\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.
forms.answer: Broken: two H-H and one O=O: $2(436)+496=1368$. Formed: four O-H bonds: $4(463)=1852$. $\Delta H_r=1368-1852=-484\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. This is for the equation as written, producing two moles of gaseous water; per mole of water the estimate is half this value.

9701-5.1.6.motivate: Why can a correct bond-energy calculation disagree with a measured reaction enthalpy?
9701-5.1.6.establish: An exact bond dissociation enthalpy belongs to a specified bond-breaking process in a specified gaseous species, such as splitting gaseous hydrogen molecules into gaseous atoms. An average bond energy is a mean; a tabulated value commonly averages a bond type over different gaseous compounds. Molecular environment affects bond energy, so the same bond type need not have the same value everywhere. Successive bond dissociations in methane also differ: the mean C–H energy in methane is one quarter of its total gaseous atomisation enthalpy, not simply the first dissociation energy. Here exact means specific to a process, not free from experimental uncertainty.
9701-5.1.6.connect: Average values make bond-energy calculations useful estimates rather than guaranteed experimental results.
9701-5.1.6.note:
- Exact bond dissociation enthalpy: a specified gaseous bond-breaking process.
- Average bond energies represent means; molecular environment matters.

discover.stem: Which statement about a tabulated average C–H bond energy is correct?

discover.explanation: An average need not match any particular bond-breaking process; the surrounding molecular structure affects the energy required.

9701-5.1.6.plain_words: An exact bond energy is for one specific bond in one specific gaseous molecule. An average bond energy is the mean for the same type of bond across different molecules. Because the surroundings of a bond change its energy, calculations using averages are estimates.

forms.name: Explain exact versus average bond energy
wordings: Explain why a value calculated using average bond energies may differ from the experimental enthalpy change.
Distinguish between exact and average bond energy.
State why the O-H bond energy is different in water and in ethanol.
forms.example:
**Explain** why the O-H bond energy in water differs from that in ethanol:

- A bond energy is affected by the atoms around the bond.
- In water the oxygen is attached to another hydrogen atom; in ethanol it is attached to a carbon atom.
- So the exact O-H bond energies differ, and a tabulated average O-H value is a mean of such values.
forms.check: Explain why a bond-energy calculation for the combustion of ethanol gives only an estimate of the enthalpy change measured by experiment. Consider the molecular-environment limitation of average bond energies; assume all reactants and products are gaseous.
forms.answer: The bond energies in a table are average values: each is the mean of a bond type measured in different molecules. The actual energy of a bond depends on its molecular environment, so it may differ from the average. The calculation is therefore an estimate and may not equal the experimental value.

rubric.point: Tabulated bond energies are average values (means).
Averaged over the same bond in different molecules or environments.

retry.check: Distinguish between the exact bond energy of H-H in $\ce{H2(g)}$ and the average bond energy of C-H.
retry.answer: The exact H-H bond energy is the energy to break one mole of that specific bond in gaseous hydrogen molecules. The average C-H bond energy is the mean of the energy of C-H bonds in different molecules, because the energy of a C-H bond depends on its environment.

rubric.point: Exact: one specific bond in a specific (gaseous) molecule.
Average: mean value for a bond type taken over different molecules or environments.

forms.name: Relate methane atomisation to mean and first C–H dissociation
wordings: Calculate the mean C–H bond energy in methane from its gaseous atomisation enthalpy.
Distinguish the first C–H dissociation from the mean over all four bonds.
forms.example: Given $\ce{CH4(g) -> C(g) + 4H(g)}$ requires $1660\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, step 1 counts four C–H bonds removed per methane molecule. Step 2 divides by four: the mean for methane is $1660/4=415\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ of C–H bonds. Step 3 distinguishes $\ce{CH4(g) -> CH3(g) + H(g)}$: this breaks only the first bond.
forms.check: A supplied gaseous atomisation enthalpy of methane is $1640\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The first dissociation $\ce{CH4(g) -> CH3(g) + H(g)}$ requires $435\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Calculate the mean C–H energy in methane and the sum of the remaining three dissociation enthalpies. Explain why the first value differs from the mean.
forms.answer: Mean C–H energy in methane $=1640/4=410\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Remaining three sum to $1640-435=1205\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Successive bonds are removed from different gaseous fragments, so individual dissociation enthalpies can differ. The first dissociation is a specified process; the mean averages all four.
forms.source: Library: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c5.1.pdf p.14; bundle ER 9701 s22 P13 Q9

rubric.point: Mean C–H bond energy in methane is 410 kJ mol−1 of bonds; accept the correct value and units without working.
Remaining three dissociations sum to 1205 kJ per mole of methane.

Successive bonds are broken in different gaseous species/fragments with different molecular environments and therefore different individual bond energies; this explains why the first dissociation need not equal the four-bond mean. The explanation must link the different species/environments to differing bond energies. Accept the bonding environment changes as H atoms are removed as explaining why successive dissociation energies need not equal the mean; require this changing environment to be linked to the bond-energy comparison, rather than an unrelated use of change.

rubric.point: Methane mean is 420 kJ per mole of bonds.
Remaining three total 1240 kJ per mole.

9701-5.1.7.motivate: A thermometer measures the solution, while the question asks about the reacting chemicals. Keep their energy transfers separate.
9701-5.1.7.establish: Find the total mass of heated water or solution, using density and combined volume when appropriate. Calculate $\Delta T=T_{\mathrm{final}}-T_{\mathrm{initial}}$ and $q_{\mathrm{solution}}=mc\Delta T$ in joules. Calculate initial reactant moles and compare them using the balanced equation to identify the limiting reactant. Use the amount actually reacted on the requested mole basis; for neutralisation use moles of water formed. If heat loss and the calorimeter heat capacity are negligible, $q_{\mathrm{reaction}}=-q_{\mathrm{solution}}$. Hence $\Delta H=-q_{\mathrm{solution}}/(1000n)$ in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. A rise in solution temperature means a negative reaction enthalpy.
9701-5.1.7.connect: Standard enthalpy definitions determine the mole basis; exothermic energy transfer determines the minus sign.
9701-5.1.7.note:
- Use total heated solution mass in $q=mc\Delta T$.
- Find limiting moles and the requested mole basis.
- $\Delta H=-q/(1000n)$ in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ when $q$ is in joules.

forms.name: Calculate energy released per gram of fuel
wordings: Calculate the total energy released per gram of fuel burnt.
Calculate the energy absorbed by the water.
Calculate the energy released when the fuel is burnt.
forms.example: A fuel of molar mass $40.0\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ is burned: $1.50\ \mathrm g$ heats $200\ \mathrm g$ water by $20.0\ \mathrm K$; only $50.0\%$ of released heat is captured. Take $c=4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. Step 1: water gains $q=200(4.18)(20.0)=16720\ \mathrm J$. Step 2: $0.500Q=16720$, so total released magnitude $Q=33440\ \mathrm J$. Step 3: per gram, $33440/1.50=22293.3\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}}\approx22.3\ \mathrm{kJ\,g^{-1}}$. Step 4: $n=1.50/40.0=0.0375\ \mathrm{mol}$, so the combustion estimate is $-33440/(1000\times0.0375)\approx-892\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Heat released is a positive magnitude; reaction enthalpy is negative. Assume complete combustion, and that the stated capture fraction includes all unmeasured heat transfers.
forms.check: $2.00\ \mathrm g$ of a fuel is burnt. Only $40.0\%$ of the energy released is absorbed by $250\ \mathrm g$ of water, whose temperature rises from $19.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ to $49.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$. Calculate the total energy released per gram of fuel. Use $c=4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The fuel has molar mass $44.0\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ and burns completely. Also calculate the reaction enthalpy per mole of fuel, assuming the capture fraction accounts for all unmeasured heat.
forms.answer: $q=250\times4.18\times30.0=31\,350\ \mathrm J$. This is $40.0\%$ of the total, so total $=31\,350\div0.400=78\,375\ \mathrm J$. Per gram: $78\,375\div2.00=39\,187.5\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}}\approx39\,200\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}}$. Fuel amount $n=2.00/44.0\ \mathrm{mol}$; reaction enthalpy $=-78375/[1000(2.00/44.0)]\approx-1.72\times10^3\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The water gains energy and the reaction loses energy.
forms.source: CAIE 9701 syllabus 5.1.7; Library: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c5.1.pdf p.17-18; CAIE 9701 w25 P11 Q8

rubric.point: Uses the mass of water, not fuel: $q=250\times4.18\times30=31\,350$ J.
Converts from the 40% absorbed to the 100% total, giving 78 375 J.
Divides by 2.00 g to get about 39 200 J per gram (39.2 kJ per gram).
Uses 2.00/44.0 mol fuel, converts joules to kilojoules and gives negative 1.72 times ten cubed kJ per mole (accept -1724.25 before rounding).

retry.check: $2.50\ \mathrm g$ of a fuel is burnt. $25.0\%$ of the energy released is absorbed by $400\ \mathrm g$ of water, whose temperature rises from $22.5\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ to $41.5\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$. Calculate the total energy released per gram of fuel. Use $c=4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. Assume complete combustion and that the stated capture fraction includes every unmeasured heat transfer.
retry.answer: $\Delta T=19.0\ \mathrm K$ and $q=400\times4.18\times19.0=31\,768\ \mathrm J$. Total energy $=31\,768\div0.250=127\,072\ \mathrm J$. Per gram: $127\,072\div2.50=50\,828.8\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}}\approx50\,800\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}}$.

rubric.point: Divides by 0.250 to get 127 072 J.
Divides by 2.50 g to get about 50 800 J per gram.

forms.name: Calculate enthalpy change per mole from solution data
wordings: Calculate the enthalpy change of reaction, in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.
Use the results to calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation.
Calculate $\Delta H$ for the reaction per mole of the stated reactant.
forms.example:
**Calculate** $\Delta H_{neut}$. $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $2.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ HCl is mixed with $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $2.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH. The temperature rises from $20.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ to $33.5\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$. Assume density $1.00\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and $c=4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

- $m=50.0\ \mathrm g$ and $\Delta T=13.5\ \mathrm K$, so $q=50.0\times4.18\times13.5=2821.5\ \mathrm J$.
- Moles of water formed $=2.00\times0.0250=0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}$.
- $\Delta H=-2821.5\div(1000\times0.0500)=-56.4\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ (3 s.f.). Assume additive volumes, a common initial temperature, complete reaction, negligible heat loss and negligible calorimeter heat capacity.
forms.check: Mix $40.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.500\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ HCl with $60.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.400\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH. Both begin at $20.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ and the mixture reaches $22.5\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$. Calculate neutralisation enthalpy per mole of water. Assume additive volumes, density $1.00\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, $c=4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, complete reaction, negligible heat loss and negligible cup heat capacity.
forms.answer: $\ce{HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)}$. Acid: $0.500(0.0400)=0.0200\ \mathrm{mol}$; alkali: $0.400(0.0600)=0.0240\ \mathrm{mol}$. HCl limits, forming $0.0200\ \mathrm{mol}$ water. The entire solution has mass $100.0\ \mathrm g$ and $\Delta T=2.5\ \mathrm K$. Thus $q_{solution}=100.0(4.18)(2.5)=1045\ \mathrm J$ and $\Delta H_{neut}=-1045/(1000\times0.0200)=-52.25\approx-52\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ (2 s.f.).
forms.source: CAIE 9701 syllabus 5.1.7; Library: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c5.1.pdf p.17-18; CAIE 9701 syllabus 5.1.7 formula

rubric.point: Uses total solution mass 100 g and rise 2.5 K to find 1045 J.
Calculates acid 0.0200 mol and alkali 0.0240 mol; identifies acid limiting and 0.0200 mol water.
Divides by moles of water, converts J to kJ and gives negative 52 kJ per mole (accept -52.25 before rounding).

retry.check: $4.00\ \mathrm g$ of ammonium nitrate ($M_r=80.0$) is dissolved in $50.0\ \mathrm g$ of water. The temperature falls from $20.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ to $13.8\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$. Calculate the enthalpy change per mole of ammonium nitrate dissolved, using $c=4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and the mass of water as the heated mass. For this simplified model ignore solute and cup heat capacities and heat exchange with the air.
retry.answer: $\Delta T=13.8-20.0=-6.2\ \mathrm K$, so $q_{water}=50.0(4.18)(-6.2)=-1295.8\ \mathrm J$. Water loses heat; dissolution gains it. Moles $=4.00/80.0=0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}$. Thus $\Delta H=-q_{water}/(1000n)=+25.9\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, endothermic.

rubric.point: Uses signed temperature change -6.2 K giving water heat -1295.8 J, or explicitly uses 1295.8 J as a loss magnitude.
Moles of ammonium nitrate = 0.0500 mol.
Gives a positive enthalpy change of +25.9 kJ per mole because the temperature fell.

forms.name: Explain calorimetry heat loss and improve insulation
wordings: Explain the effect of heat loss on calculated exothermic enthalpy.
Suggest an improvement to reduce heat loss and justify it.
forms.example: An endothermic dissolution cools an insulated cup below room temperature. Some heat then enters from the warmer room before the minimum temperature is recorded. With the reacted amount fixed, this heat gain makes the observed temperature fall smaller in magnitude. Using q=mcΔT and ΔH=−q/n, the inferred positive reaction enthalpy is therefore too small. For illustration, if the ideal fall is 6.0 K but heat gain reduces it to 4.0 K, the inferred enthalpy is 4.0/6.0 of the insulated value. Assume complete dissolution and no other significant error.
forms.check: A gas-producing exothermic reaction gives $\Delta H=-35\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ in an open cup, using only solution heat. Assume complete reaction and correct moles; heat loss to cooler surroundings is the only significant error. Relative to an insulated measurement, explain the direction of the error. Suggest a suitable improvement and explain why sealing the cup with a bung is unsuitable.
forms.answer: The measured temperature rise and solution heat are too small. The released magnitude is underestimated, so -35 kJ per mole is less negative (closer to zero) than the insulated value. Use a polystyrene cup, extra insulation or an insulating lid that permits gas to escape. An airtight bung traps the gas and can cause pressure to build up.
forms.source: Cambridge International 9701 June 2024 examiner report, Paper 52 Q1(i), https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/567188-june-2024-examiner-report.pdf; Library: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c5.1.pdf pp.16–18 for calorimeter context; direction of bias follows q=mc delta T under the stated assumptions; Library: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c5.1.pdf pp.17–18; endothermic heat-gain example derived from q=mcΔT and ΔH=−q/n under stated assumptions.

rubric.point: Heat loss to cooler surroundings makes the measured temperature rise or heat gained by the solution too small; the reduction must refer to the measured temperature rise or solution heat, not to reduced heat loss after insulation.
Calculated exothermic enthalpy is less negative / too close to zero; the heat-release magnitude is too small.
Suitable insulation or an insulating lid reduces heat loss while permitting gas escape.
A bung can trap the gas and cause pressure buildup.

retry.check: A repeated gas-producing exothermic experiment uses the same reacting amount, but adds insulation and a vented lid. Assume both reactions go to completion and insulation is the only change. Predict the changes in temperature rise and calculated reaction enthalpy. Would a gas-tight stopper be an equivalent improvement?
retry.answer: Less heat escapes, so the temperature rise increases and the calculated enthalpy becomes more negative, nearer the insulated value. A gas-tight stopper is unsuitable because gas must escape rather than accumulate pressure.

rubric.point: Temperature rise increases as heat loss decreases.
Calculated enthalpy becomes more negative for the same reacted amount.
Rejects gas-tight stopper because trapped gas raises pressure.
